newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico stock gains boosted by Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: Mexico stock gains boosted by Wall Street.

text.p: Mexican stocks ended higher after zizagging in light trading as caution over volatile U.S. markets alternated with strong domestic fundamentals.

"A very strange day on Wall Street, but it ended up so we did too, fine, but fundamentally the bourse is very strong, that's why we fended off falling prices in New York," a Mexico City desk trader said.
The leading IPC share index ended up 11.17 points, or 0.30 percent, at 3,752.47. Volume was slow at 55.8 million shares traded.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 48.72 points at 6,526.07. Analysts noted the bourse was in positive territory even when the Dow had fallen more than 70 points.

"We are optimistic. We are decoupling ourselves from New York, Mexico's fundamentals are good. Furthermore, the market is cheap, but you need to tread carefully when picking stocks because growth is not even," an equity analyst said.

Telmex L, which accounted for one quarter of all shares traded in Mexico, weighed most heavily on the bourse and ended down two centavos (less than 1 cent) at 15.64 pesos ($1.97). Its ADRs closed up 1/8 at 39-1/8 on Wall Street.
Dealers said a stronger peso encouraged arbitrage trading, whereby brokers sold L shares in Mexico to buy ADRs in New York.
News the U.S. Deaprtment of Commerce had decided to raise anti-dumping tariffs on Mexican cement exports led to a volatile session for the three cement makers included in the IPC index.

Cemex B shares ended up 25 centavos (3 cents) at 31.95 pesos ($4.02), while the CPO series gained 40 centavos (5 cents) to 29.00 pesos ($3.65). The B and CPO series were the third- and fourth-most traded stocks during the session.
Apasco meanwhile gained two pesos (25 cents) to 54.80 pesos ($6.90).
Analysts noted the tariffs would hit neither company hard, as Cemex had a diversified export base, and Apasco exported little to the U.S. market.

Analysts said the anti-dumping measures would, however, hurt Grupo Cementos de Chihuahua (GCC), a cement maker in northern Mexico that depends heavily on exports to the United States. GCC ended down six centavos (1 cent) at 7.90 pesos (99 cents).
